doc.title: Hal Galper interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 27, 2022

title: Apprenticeship, oral tradition, and the missing culture
summary: Galper argues schools teach information but only apprenticeship teaches its use, describes levels of masters, and says the supporting culture is gone; he recalls Sonny Stitt's penalties.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: That speaks to the system then. I have my own — I came up with my own system. What they did is they destroyed it. The white people who run the academia there destroyed music. Destroyed jazz. You’ve got these older white men making all these decisions about music that really comes from a black culture. And this is a really — I’m on my soapbox on this because traditionally people talk about information and process. Right? You’ve got to learn the information and then you’ve got to learn how to use it. All right?

So you learn the information in school, you learn how to use it in the apprenticeship system. All right? That’s the only place to learn is the apprenticeship system. You have to play the stuff. You have to try it out and you have to be playing with a master. You can’t — David Baker said, “You don’t learn anything playing with your peers.” You have to play — and all the masters that I played with, apprenticed with, they all had awe. They were awesome. And if they told you do something you stood up and saluted and did it whether you understood it or not, and sometimes it took you ten years to understand what they told you to do, but they never explained anything. The reason being is they needed you to figure it out yourself because the oral tradition is based on one premise, development of personal voice. That is not part of the educational system, the development of personal voice. But the oral tradition — there are 6,700 different oral tradition, non English oral traditions in the world. It’s been around for — I mean the first song flute was 20,000 years old. You know music has been around, unwritten, for 20,000 years. And the Gutenberg Bible screwed all that up because now they could print music and see the notes and make it symbols instead of real sounds. And they get the symbols — it’s symbols you know. They give the symbols value. It’s the sound that has value. So the third leg that’s missing is the culture and that has to do with your question. It’s the culture, music always expresses the culture of the moment. And the culture at the time that I was coming up doesn’t exist anymore. It’s completely fragmented. That has weakened the music tremendously. It’s fragmented. Everybody’s on their own going for the — nobody’s listening to themselves. And I’ve even heard at New School the students frown on you if you swing. So it’s the culture that’s missing. The culture that exists now does not support the music. It’s the culture. I mean there’s a stratification of the culture as well as stratification of the music which both work at the same time. You’re on a certain level, all right, you don’t talk to the people on the next level. I can’t think of a time I initiated a conversation with a master. I never did. They talked to me. You didn’t talk to a master because they were somewhere else. Their concerns had nothing to do with your existence. You’re down here at level three and they’re up at level ten. You can talk to level four maybe, and maybe get a little something from level five. And the same thing is happening socially in the black culture. You’re not supposed to bypass anybody. Obama really pissed off the black community in Chicago when he ran against their older black favorite. He jumped over him to get this position on a commission or something and it really pissed off the community because the tradition is you don’t skip a level. You earn it. You don’t get to the next level until you’ve done the work to get to it, and then your work gets recognized and you’re on the next level with a whole new set of different questions and a whole set of different answers and you don’t even know that there’s another level coming up. And finally when you’ve got finished with that level you’re in

the next level and there’s a whole different set of questions and answers. It just never stops. And there’s a musical structure that goes right along with it. That’s how the discipline was kept. The masters kept the discipline. There’s no discipline anymore. If you didn’t do something right — I was playing in a house band with Sonny Stitt, amazing gig for two weeks. He didn’t like what the drummer was doing and made him play up on the bell for two weeks. His arm is out like that for two weeks, killing him. They penalize you. If you didn’t do something right, you didn’t do what they said, they penalized you until you got it together. So they beat you up physically, I mean musically. Usually that’s what happened they just crushed you, you know, they were just so great. Phil — Phil could just crush me in a second. I’m an ant next to him. I will never do fours or exchanges with Phil. I did it once, never again, never again. He just blew me out of the water you know. That’s something for later on, maybe I’ll get that together you know. It’s an interesting thing. That cultural support is missing. That’s the problem here. Process orientation and the culture. That’s the situation.
